title: The Crow and the Tiny Prince
markdown:
Not all stories begin in cottages. This one began with a jolt, a shudder, and a clang that rattled feathers down to the tail.

Aboard a rickety rescue pod — more close calls than polite landings — two unlikely companions were strapped in. Lark, a crow of considerable mechanical talent, beak usually dusted with engine grease. Timo, a prince from a planet so tiny you would need a telescope made of wishes to glimpse it: no bigger than a thumb, skin shimmering like a dragonfly wing, eyes the depth of a starry night.

They had been hurrying to pick up a lost probe, important space-junk gone wandering. A rogue asteroid, a grumpy chunk of rock, sent them spinning like a child's top. Instead of a station with warm tea and polite pilots, they tumbled onto something cold. Not winter-cold. A deep penetrating chill that seemed to whisper of the void.

"Caw! What in the blazes was that?" Lark's voice was pebbles in a tin can. He unbuckled with a practiced flap, greasy feathers ruffled.

Timo unstrapped from his tiny harness. "Oh dear. That was rather… jumbled." He peered from the viewport. "Is this a cloud?"

"A cloud?" Lark scoffed, waddling to the window. "That's an iceberg. And that — that's an ammonia sea."

Out there a sea is not always salt. Sometimes methane gone liquid in the intense cold, or, as here, ammonia: a cosmic soup you would not swim in. Everything frozen solid, sparkling and strange.

The iceberg was a continent of ice: jagged white peaks scraping a pale sky, blue-tinged crevasses like frozen wounds. Thin biting air, a faint sharp scent, utterly alien. It tickled Lark's beak. Timo hummed a little faster, a slightly nervous tune.

"Right." Lark ruffled, trying to sound confident. "Assess the damage. Then a signal. Very loud. Very clear. The kind that would make space-whales perk up, even if they don't exist."

Timo, heart bright as his skin, hummed his tinkling melody. "Perhaps we can explore a little first? It is quite picturesque. Who knows what wonders?"

Therefore they stepped onto the ice. It crunched under Lark's claws, a satisfying echo, and barely whispered under Timo's three-toed feet. Pale ethereal light seemed to come from everywhere. Lark poked the pod, muttering about hull integrity and flux capacitors in an ammonia atmosphere. Timo was fascinated by crystals like a million diamonds a giant had scattered.

"Look, Lark! A frozen whisper. As if the ice is trying to tell a story."

Lark's beak scraped a shard. "Looks more like a good way to trip and fall on your beak." Even he had to admit, shielding his eyes, it was a wonder.

They spent what felt like hours, or moments — time stretches, in space, when you are trying to survive — exploring. Hidden caves where ammonia had frozen into glassy stalactites that dripped an invisible moisture. Patches of ice with a faint inner glow, as if holding captured starlight. They found a hollow where the wind made a flute of a crevasse, a note so low Lark felt it in his keel-bone. Timo collected nothing; his pockets were too small, and besides, ice would only become a sad puddle in a warmer room. Beautiful. A little lonely. The ammonia sea went on forever, an endless frozen mystery.

But the signal amplifier needed height, a clear line to the nearest star lane. The iceberg was a pancake, not much of a hill. Shouting secrets to the stars from the bottom of a bowl. Lark tried a lower ridge first; the beam would have hit a shoulder of ice and bounced into nowhere useful. Therefore he scratched his head with a grease-stained claw — and a peculiar wind began. Not gusty. A steady deep breath of cold that pushed and lifted, ice groaning underfoot. An ammonia-wind storm. It piled the ice, an invisible hand sculpting, a steep ridge growing and growing.

"Lark, what is happening?" Timo clung to his back as the berg shifted. Ice cracked like an old tree in a gale. (He had almost said Corvus, a textbook name for crows, and caught himself; Lark was Lark.)

"Hold on tight, Prince!" Wings spread for balance, heart thumping. "It's the wind. Building us a tower. A temporary skyscraper of frost."

Wind howled. Crystals swirled, a blizzard of diamonds, visibility a few feet. For a moment the whole iceberg might break, swallow them in the unforgiving sea. Timo shut his eyes; the tinkle became a low worried hum through Lark's feathers. Lark, bristled, mind racing on structural integrity — load, shear, the unpleasant maths of a pancake becoming a tower — kept his eyes on the ridge. Perilous. A test they had not scheduled. The pod, below, looked like a dropped seed. If the ridge failed, there would be no second amplifier.

"Don't worry, little one." A deep rumble, knees a little wobbly. "We're a team. Crow and Prince against the cold."

Finally the wind sighed across the frozen expanse and subsided. They had been pushed to the peak of the new ridge. Precarious. Dizzying. Perfect, if you liked heights and did not mind the way the ice ticked as it settled. Lark, claws usually so steady now trembling, connected the amplifier, checked the couplings twice the way he would in a proper workshop, and aimed it at distant cold stars.

"Come on, you rusty old thing." A tap of the beak. "Sing us home. Loud and clear."

A thin beam of energy into the void, a fragile thread. They waited. Silence, vast, broken by ice settling. Timo sat on Lark's head, scanning the dark. The amplifier hummed, then hiccuped, then hummed again. Lark rapped a coupling with his beak until the hiccup stopped. He did not trust a machine that sounded like it was thinking of a nap.

Waiting was the hardest part. Doubts crept like frost on glass. They had done their best. That was all. Lark counted the seconds the way he counted bolts in a workshop: one, two, skip the ones that were already tight. Timo hummed a thinner melody, the sort you use when you are pretending not to watch the sky. The ridge ticked. Somewhere below, the pod's hull contracted with a small unhappy ping. An ammonia flake landed on Lark's wing and stayed there, a tiny star that refused to melt.

"If nobody comes," Timo said, very quietly, "we still have the caves. And the flute-crevasse. And each other, which is a rather small crew, but a crew."

"If nobody comes," Lark said, "I shall invent a louder amplifier out of ice and bad language. But somebody will come. Beams do not like to travel alone."

Then a speck on the horizon, faint against ink. It grew until it was a ship, hull like a polished pearl, engines a gentle song. Drawn by the signal. Lark's claws unclenched one by one. Timo stood up on his shoulder so as not to miss a porthole.

They were taken aboard, bundled into warm softly glowing chambers, given strange sweet nectar that tasted of sunshine and honey. A medic who had never seen a prince the size of a thumb offered Timo a cup the size of a thimble and looked embarrassed when it still sloshed. Lark left a grease print on a clean bulkhead and did not apologise. Watching the iceberg recede, a little sadness: the end of a shared perilous journey. The ridge they had stood on was already slumping, the wind's tower forgetting itself.

"It was a grand adventure, wasn't it, Lark?" Timo whispered, iridescent skin dimming as the white speck shrank.

Lark nodded, a quiet rumble almost a sigh. "Grand. And rather chilly. Never thought I'd trade my greasy workshop for an ammonia sea." He looked at the tiny prince on his shoulder. "We made it through. Next time we pick a probe that stays on the map."

They exchanged tokens: a polished shard of ice, a shimmering scale. Promises to remember. They did not need a lecture on unlikely friendship. The shard would melt eventually, in warmer air. The scale would keep a little cold in it, if you held it close. That was enough, on a drifting berg in the strangest of seas.
